conventions.convention: The Markov property is asserted only relative to a named filtration (F_n); the natural filtration is a specialization, and the property relative to a larger filtration is a strictly stronger assertion, not a change of notation. All conditional-probability identities are equalities of almost-everywhere classes, with no pointwise regular version selected.

Conditional independence is the bounded-product identity E[f(Y)g(Z)|G] = E[f(Y)|G]E[g(Z)|G] for all bounded measurable f,g, and the sigma-algebra form uses bounded variables from each side; it is an a.e.-class statement, and the useful equivalent form is invariance of the conditional law of one side when the other is adjoined to the conditioning sigma-algebra.

Kernel composition is chronological, K then L: (KL)(s,A) = integral of L(t,A) over K(s,dt); iterated kernels start at K^0 = identity and K^{n+1} = K^n K, so K^{m+n} = K^m K^n and the zero cases m = 0, n = 0 are included.
Strong Markov future terms are the slice sums sum_n 1_{tau=n} H(X_n, X_{n+1}, ...) and sum_n 1_{tau=n} h(X_n), both set to zero on {tau = infinity}; no value X_infinity is defined or used.

Absorption replaces rows at x in D by the Dirac row delta_x; killing sends a start outside D immediately to an adjoined cemetery point Delta which is absorbing, on the sigma-algebra E_Delta = E plus the sets A union {Delta}; a start in D is killed exactly when the kernel would leave D.

Normal laws are permitted to be degenerate: N(m,0) is the Dirac mass at m, zero variance is allowed, and multivariate normal laws with singular covariance are retained; a Gaussian process is one whose every finite linear combination is normal.

Standard Brownian motion requires B_0 = 0 a.s., independent N(0,t_j - t_{j-1}) increments along every strictly increasing finite list 0 = t_0 < ... < t_n, and one measurable probability-one event of pathwise continuity on [0,infinity); no filtration, completion or right-continuity is included, and continuity is never inferred from finite-dimensional laws.

Continuous path space C([0,infinity),R) carries the weighted uniform-on-compacts metric d_uoc(f,g) = sum_n 2^{-n}(1 and max_{t<=n}|f-g|); its Borel sigma-algebra equals the sigma-algebra generated by the rational coordinate maps, and all path-space laws are compared on that sigma-algebra, nowhere larger.

Wiener measure is obtained from a standard Brownian motion only after the zero-repair on one supplied continuity event A: the path is B on A and the zero path off A; the unrestored process is never treated as a path-space random element.

Martingale identities are asserted against the uncompleted natural filtration, in the all-pairs form E[M_t | F_s] = M_s a.s. for every 0 <= s <= t; no path continuity, right-continuity or completeness of the filtration is implied by the word continuous-time.

Choice is declared explicitly at the head of each statement that consumes conditional-expectation classes, standard-Borel disintegration, arbitrary-index extension or the normal-law interfaces; the kernel algebra, killed/absorbed verification, positive-semidefiniteness and even-moment computations and the one-parameter continuity criterion are choice-free, and the Polish path-space lemma assumes only countable choice.

load_bearing.statement: A real process B is a standard Brownian motion if: (1) B_0 = 0 almost surely; (2) for every finite list 0 = t_0 < t_1 < ... < t_n the increments B_{t_j} - B_{t_{j-1}} are mutually independent with laws N(0, t_j - t_{j-1}); and (3) there is one measurable event A with P(A) = 1 such that t -> B_t(omega) is continuous on [0,infinity) for every omega in A.

A real process X is a Gaussian process if for every n >= 1, every finite time list t_1,...,t_n and every real a_1,...,a_n the linear combination sum_j a_j X_{t_j} has a normal law N(m, sigma^2), variance zero allowed; equivalently every finite evaluation vector has a possibly singular multivariate normal law.

Assume Choice. An adapted process has the indicator Markov property with kernel K if and only if for every bounded E-measurable real f and every n >= 0, E[f(X_{n+1}) | F_n] = Kf(X_n) almost surely, where Kf(x) = integral of f(y) K(x,dy).

Assume the axiom of choice. An adapted E-valued process X is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel K relative to (F_n) if for every n >= 0 and A in E, P(X_{n+1} in A | F_n) = K(X_n,A) almost surely; the natural-filtration case is a specialization, and a larger filtration is a stronger assertion.

Assume Choice. For a real process X with X_0 = 0 almost surely, TFAE: (1) X is centered Gaussian with Cov(X_s,X_t) = min(s,t) for all s,t >= 0; (2) for every finite list 0 = t_0 < ... < t_n the increments X_{t_j} - X_{t_{j-1}} are mutually independent with laws N(0, t_j - t_{j-1}).

For a complete separable metric target S and an S-valued process X with E[d(X_t,X_s)^alpha] <= C_T |t-s|^{1+beta} on 0 <= s,t <= T, X has a continuous modification Y, and one version can be chosen so that, on one probability-one event, its paths are Holder on every compact interval for every exponent 0 < gamma < beta/alpha.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure mu and probability kernel K on an arbitrary measurable space (E,E), the canonical path space (E^{N_0}, E^{tensor N_0}) carries a unique probability P_mu under which the coordinate maps form a Markov chain with initial law mu and transition kernel K.

With the zero-repaired Brownian path map W(omega)(t) = B_t(omega) on the continuity event A and 0 off A, W is a Borel random element of C([0,infinity),R) with the uniform-on-compacts topology, and its law P composed with W^{-1} is Wiener measure, a probability measure whose coordinate process has the Brownian finite-dimensional distributions.

For countable S with sigma-algebra 2^S, transition matrix p and bounded f, Pf(x) = sum_y p(x,y) f(y) and Lf(x) = Pf(x) - f(x) = sum_y p(x,y)(f(y) - f(x)), the last series being absolutely convergent; constants have zero generator and the definition uses no choice.

Assume Choice. For measurable spaces (E_n,E_n), a probability mu_0 on E_0 and history-dependent probability kernels K_n from E_0 x ... x E_n to E_{n+1}, there is a unique probability P on the product whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals; in the homogeneous last-coordinate specialization the coordinates form a K-chain with initial law mu_0.

Assume Choice. Y and Z are conditionally independent given G if and only if E[g(Z) | G join sigma(Y)] = E[g(Z) | G] almost surely for every bounded measurable g; conditional independence is preserved by measurable maps of either variable and by adjoining a G-measurable random element to either side.

concerns.concern: Step 1.1 asserts '|Z_H|, |R_h| <= ||H||_inf, so both variables are integrable', but only R_h is shown F_tau-measurable (via the stopped-variable supplier). Measurability of the slice sum Z_H = sum_n 1_{tau=n} H(X_n, X_{n+1}, ...) is never stated, although integrability requires it and step 2.1's dominated-convergence passage to 1_A Z_H presupposes it. The gap closes in one line (each summand is measurable and at most one is nonzero), but the proof as written does not address it.

The closing sentence of the Statement ('Thus, conditional on the information at the hit, the shifted chain has the canonical path law started from the hit state') and step 2.1 ('it identifies the conditional path law, not only its one-time marginals') assert an identification of a conditional law, but the item and its declared dependencies provide only the bounded-functional identity: no regular conditional distribution is produced and no statement that x -> P_x(B) is measurable (the kernel property in the initial state) is available in the item or in [F1]-[F2]. The display itself is correct and fully supported; only the prose identification outruns the declared machinery.

The Statement defines h(x) := E_x[H(X_0, X_1, ...)] for a general K-chain X on an arbitrary space, but the subscript-x law P_x = P_{delta_x} is fixed only by def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain, which is not among the declared deps, and the proof silently realises h through the canonical law P_x of [F5]. Standard notation, but the notational commitment to the canonical law should be declared or cross-referenced.

Statement: 'After redefining the paths of Y to be zero on its common exceptional continuity event, its path-space law is Wiener measure.' Read literally (zero the paths on the probability-one continuity event) this gives the zero path almost surely and hence not Wiener measure; the intended reading is the Wiener-measure repair of def-wiener-measure, namely zeroing off the continuity event, as step 4.1 does. The word 'exceptional' is carrying the meaning of 'complement' and the sentence should say so.

Statement: 'let X be adapted to (F_n). Then X is a p-chain if and only if ...', but f(X_n), Lf(X_n) and the phrase p-chain all presuppose that X takes values in the countable state space S; S-valuedness of the adapted process is nowhere stated (the Given repeats only 'the adapted process X'). Type-checking forces the intended hypothesis, but it is an unstated hypothesis of the statement.
